The Story of Gandharvasena

I bow to the feet of Lord Jina, the bestower of all happiness, and I write the story of the foolish Gandharvasena, who was caught in the claws of death through her excessive attachment to the art of singing.

King Gandharvadatt of Pataliputra (Patna) and Queen Gandharvadatta had a daughter named Gandharvasena. She was highly skilled in the art of music and had taken a vow: "Whoever defeats me in singing shall be my lord, and I shall become his wife." Many Kshatriya princes came, drawn by her beauty and fame like bees to a flower, but all had to return disappointed. No one could match Gandharvasena in song.

One day, a teacher named Panchal, who was a great master of music, heard of Gandharvasena and wished to see her. He came to Patna with his five hundred disciples and stayed in a garden. It was summer, and after a long journey, Panchal was tired. He told his students, "If anyone comes, wake me up," and fell asleep in the cool shade of a tree. His students then went off to see the city.

When Gandharvasena heard of Panchal's arrival and his scholarship, she came to see him. She found him sleeping with many veenas (musical instruments) around him. She understood that he must be a great scholar. But when she saw drool flowing from his mouth, she felt such disgust that she could not even look at him. She turned away and went back to her palace, having the tree where he slept worshipped with sandalwood and flowers as a sign of respect for his learning, but refusing to wake him.

After Gandharvasena left, Panchal woke up and found the tree worshipped. He asked a student what had happened, and the student told him about a woman who had come, worshipped the tree, and left. Panchal understood that Gandharvasena had come and gone. He thought, "This is not right. Sleep has ruined everything. But now it is too late to turn back. I must try."

He went to the king and requested a place to stay. The king granted it. Panchal then sent a message to Gandharvasena, challenging her to a musical contest. Gandharvasena accepted. The contest was held in the royal court, with the king and all the nobles as judges. Panchal sang first, and his music was so divine that everyone was entranced. When Gandharvasena tried to respond, she found herself unable to match his skill. She was defeated.

True to her vow, Gandharvasena married Panchal. But she was unhappy, for she had been forced to marry a man she found repulsive. Her pride in her own singing had led her to make a vow she could not keep, and now she was bound to a man she despised. She spent her life in misery, realising too late that excessive attachment to any skill or art can lead to suffering.

This story teaches that pride in one's abilities can lead to foolish vows and unfortunate outcomes. Gandharvasena's obsession with being the best singer led her to make a vow that ultimately caused her unhappiness. The wise should cultivate humility and not let pride in their skills lead them into traps.
